column4: Description

Examine river cobbles to find one with the right weight and shape to fit comfortably in your palm. Our ancestors spent two million years perfecting this selection - a good hammerstone becomes an extension of the arm.

Strike one stone against another at the correct angle to detach thin, sharp flakes. This simple act - discovered 2.6 million years ago - was humanitys first deliberate tool creation. The flakes produced are waste to the toolmaker but treasure to those who recognize their cutting potential.
Remove flakes from one end of a cobble to create a rough chopping edge - the defining tool of Oldowan technology. For over a million years, this was the height of human innovation.

Carefully retouch a sharp flake to create a steep, sturdy scraping edge. The Oldowan knappers discovered that different angles served different purposes - the scraper was one of humanitys first specialized tools.
Strike flakes from a flint nodule. Flint fractures according to precise physical laws, producing edges sharper than surgical steel - a vast improvement over common stone.
Carefully retouch a flint flake to create a durable blade with one sharp edge and one blunt edge for safe handling. The conchoidal fracture of flint produces edges only molecules thick.

Shape a large flint nodule from both faces to create a symmetrical teardrop form - the hallmark of Acheulean technology. This elegant design produces four times more cutting edge than Oldowan choppers.
Roast meat over the fire until done. The control of fire transformed human nutrition - cooking breaks down proteins, kills parasites, and releases more calories.
Carefully peel thin layers of papery bark from a birch branch. The bark separates most easily in early spring when the sap rises - a technique humans have used for over fifty thousand years.
Tear and shred birch bark to separate the inner bast fibers. These long, flexible strands were the basis of Neanderthal cordage technology - evidence of which dates back at least 50,000 years.

Twist fibers clockwise into yarn, then twist two yarns counter-clockwise together. This opposing twist locks the fibers in tension - a deceptively complex technique that enabled snares, hafted tools, and countless other technologies.
Select a hardwood branch and sharpen one end to a point using a stone flake. This most basic of tools unlocks the calories stored in underground tubers.
Find a heavy branch with good heft for striking. Sometimes the simplest weapon is best.
Collect fine, dry materials that will catch a spark - shredded bark, dried grass, or fungal amadou.
Carve a straight hardwood spindle and prepare a softwood fireboard with a notched depression. The hand drill is one of humanitys oldest fire-starting methods.
A bow-driven spindle generates more heat with less effort than a hand drill. The addition of a bearing block and bow transforms fire-making from exhausting work to reliable technique.
Remove flesh and fat from a fresh hide using a stone scraper. Speed is essential - an untreated hide begins rotting within hours.
Work animal brains into a scraped hide, then smoke it to produce soft, washable buckskin. Every animal has just enough brain to tan its own hide.
Bind a sharpened point to a straight shaft using cordage. The first composite tools combined materials with different properties.
Attach a carefully knapped flint point to a spear shaft. The flint tip penetrates far deeper than wood alone.
Gather a single piece of leather and tie it with sinew to create a basic container.
Shape a bow stave and string it with twisted sinew or plant fiber. The bow stores energy for instant release.
Attach fletching and points to straight shafts. Fletching stabilizes flight through drag.
Carve a hooked throwing stick that effectively extends the arm, doubling spear velocity.
Make lightweight darts designed for atlatl throwing - longer and more flexible than hand-thrown spears.
Create a multi-pronged spear for fishing in shallows. The spread of points compensates for light refraction in water.
Weave a conical basket trap that allows fish to enter but not escape.
Create tiny, geometric stone bladelets for composite tools. These small pieces maximize cutting edge per unit of precious stone.
Cut and stitch leather pieces into a garment covering the torso. Sewn clothing enabled human expansion into cold climates.
Stitch leather leg coverings for travel through brush and cold weather.
Create foot coverings from thick leather with sewn soles.
Grind and polish a bone splinter into a fine needle with a drilled eye. This tiny tool enabled the revolution of sewn clothing.
Hollow a large log using fire and stone adzes. This labor-intensive process creates humanitys first true watercraft.
Grind and polish a greenstone blank against sandstone until smooth. Polished axes cut faster and last longer than flaked tools.
Layer horn, wood, and sinew to create a bow more powerful than its size suggests. A masterwork of materials science.
Construct a triggered trap that drops a heavy weight on prey. Passive hunting that works while you sleep.
Create a noose trap that tightens when triggered. Snares catch small game with minimal effort.
Interlace flexible plant materials into a lightweight container for gathering and storage.
Clean an animal bladder or stomach for use as a water container.
Fold and stitch birch bark into a waterproof vessel.
Construct a leather container for carrying and protecting arrows.
Pinch and coil clay into a simple vessel, then fire it in an open fire.
Create a thick-walled ceramic vessel designed to withstand direct flame.
Build a large ceramic container for storing grain and other goods.
Form a shallow ceramic vessel for serving and eating.
Shape a flat stone for grinding grain into flour.
Set sharp flint bladelets into a curved wooden handle for harvesting grain.
Attach a flat stone blade to a wooden handle for tilling soil.
Create a weighted spindle for spinning fiber into thread.
Draw out and twist wool fibers into continuous thread.
Spin processed flax fibers into linen thread.
Interlace threads on a loom to create fabric.
Construct a basic frame loom for weaving cloth.
Cut and stitch cloth into a comfortable garment.
Cold-work native copper into simple shapes through hammering.
Melt copper in a crucible and cast a pointed tool for leather working.
Extract copper from malachite ore using high-temperature smelting.
Combine copper and tin to create bronze - harder than either metal alone.
Cast and hammer a bronze axe head, then haft it to a wooden handle.
Craft a leaf-shaped bronze blade - the first true swords.
Cast a socketed bronze spearhead for mounting on a wooden shaft.
Hammer out a bronze knife blade and fit it with a handle.
Craft a heavy hammer for metalworking.
Layer and harden leather into protective body armor.
Construct a wooden shield faced with rawhide for protection in combat.
Hammer sheet bronze into a protective helmet.
Create a shield with bronze facing for superior protection.
Shape clay on a potters wheel for uniform, thin-walled vessels.
Construct a rotating platform for throwing pottery.
Construct a two-wheeled war chariot - the ultimate Bronze Age weapon platform.
Assemble overlapping bronze scales onto a leather backing.
Hammer bronze into shin guards for leg protection.
Apply mineral glazes to pottery before firing for a waterproof finish.
Fuse sand and soda ash at high temperature to create glass.
Form molten glass into decorative beads.
Reduce iron ore to metal in a bloomery furnace.
Hammer slag from iron bloom to produce wrought iron.
Pack iron with charcoal and heat to absorb carbon, creating steel.
Hammer wrought iron into a sword blade.
Create a superior sword from steel - harder and more resilient than iron.
Hammer iron into an axe head.
Create a socketed iron spearhead.
Hammer small iron points for arrows.
Attach iron arrowheads and fletching to shafts.
Interlink iron rings into flexible armor.
Shape iron into a protective helmet.
Create a shield with iron boss and rim.
Hammer iron into a U-shaped shoe to protect horse hooves.
Draw iron into nails for construction.
Cast and shape a heavy iron anvil for smithing.
Construct leather bellows for increasing forge temperature.
Create iron tongs for handling hot metal.
